job: perfect tense of an intransitive verb, formed with be and the past participle, expressing the state reached
definition: In intransitive verbs, forming tenses of the perfect; in later use chiefly with verbs of motion such as come, go, rise, set, fall, arrive, depart, grow, etc., expressing a condition or state attained at the time of speaking, rather than the action of reaching it, e.g. ‘the sun is set’, ‘our guests are gone’, ‘Babylon is fallen’, ‘the children are all grown up’. Now largely replaced by have following the pattern of transitive verbs (OED be v., sense IV.16.b).

(Milton, Paradise Regain'd ii. 140, 1671); ModE "His parents were grown old." (C. M. Yonge, Cameos 1st Series ix. 58, 1868); latest "The..purple lupine blossoms are gone forever." (J. R. Smith, San Francisco's Lost Landmarks, 2005).

job: to guard, defend or keep safe, and to keep a threat off (verb); a keeper or guard (noun)
definition: Verb: to guard, stand guard over; to keep in safety, take care of; to defend, protect (OED ward v.1, sense 1.a); to defend or protect from (1.b); to avert, keep off harm or danger (7); intransitive, to take up a position of defence, take precautions against (8, obsolete). Noun: a watchman, guard, keeper, warden (OED ward n.1, obsolete, Old English to 1473).
usage_notes: Patterns (OED ward v.1 and ward n.1): VERB sense 1.a, to guard or keep safe with a direct object, OE-LMdE: OE "Þa Englisce men þe wærdedon þære sæ." (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, MS Laud, annal 1087); ME (c1384) "Thei goynge forth, kepten, or wardiden, the sepulcre." Sense 1.d, intransitive, to keep guard, ME-LMdE: 1390 "And in this hous to loke and warde Was Minotaurus put in warde." Sense 2, to rule or act as guardian, OE-1400: OE "Nabochodonossor.. weardode wide rice." (Caedmon's Dan. 665); 1390 "tok this child into his warde, And seide he wolde him kepe and warde." (Gower, Confessio Amantis I. 345). Sense 7, to avert or keep off harm, a1586-: a1586 "While they did ward sun-beames with shady bay." (Sir P. Sidney, Arcadia); 1810 "I, only I, can ward their fate." Sense 8, intransitive, to take precautions against (obsolete, 1230-1753): 1709 "To ward against the coming Blow." (M. Prior, Paulo Purganti 100); 1726 "Regard must be had..in cold Countries to ward against the bleak Northwind." (G. Leoni, trans. L. B. definition: The office or position of guardian: the guardianship of a minor, in Feudal Law the guardianship and custody of the person and lands of a minor with all profits accruing during his or her minority (OED wardship n., sense 1.a); guardianship, protection, custody, chiefly figurative (1.b); the state or condition of being a ward (2.a); transferred and figurative (2.b).

Russe in Paston Letters & Papers, 2004, II. 104); EMdE 1540 "Personnes, to whom the kinges highnes shall graunt the custodye and wardeship of any of his graces wardes." Blackstone, Commentaries II. v. 67); LMdE 1884 "Sect. 35..assigns to the Chancery Division the wardship of infants." (Law Times 77. 309/1). Sense 1.b, general guardianship, protection, custody, chiefly figurative, 1631-: 1631 "[He] freed this kingdome from the wardship of the Peeres." (J. historical_spelling: wardein, wardeyn, wardayn, wardain, wardane, wardens, warden, wardened
job: the guardian or keeper, used as a title (noun); to watch over as a warden (verb)
definition: Noun: one who guards, protects, or defends; occasionally a guardian angel (OED warden n.1, sense 1.a, obsolete); one who has the care of something specified, a keeper (2.a, obsolete except poetic); and many offices from the guardian of an heir to the head of a college or an air-raid warden. Verb: to watch over or guard as a warden (OED warden v., from 1910).
usage_notes: Patterns (OED warden n.1 and warden v.): NOUN sense 1.a, one who guards, protects, or defends; occasionally a guardian angel (obsolete, ?c1225-1513): ?c1225 "Wat crist ure vchan. to swa gentil wardein bereð to lute menske." (Ancrene Riwle, MS Cleopatra C.vi, 232); c1290 "Þere in seint Iohanes warde is swete moder he tok,..hire wardein he was aftur also þat he to heouene i-wende." (John 31 in S.E. Leg. 403); c1400 "There is none so caitif pilgrym that he ne hath assigned hym a wardeyne the hour of his byrthe." (Pylgr. Sowle i. vii.). Sense 2.a, one who has the care of something specified; a keeper (obsolete except poetic, a1290-): a1290 "Þe hayward nom and bleu his horn, For he wes wardein of þat corn." (S. Eustace 230); 1362 "For Rihtfoliche Resoun schulde rulen ou alle, And kuynde wit be wardeyn oure weolþe to kepe." (W. Langland, Piers Plowman A. i. 53); a1400 "Garners and granges fild wit sede,..In ilk sted a sere wardain." (Cursor Mundi, MS Vespasian, 4691); 1871 "Of all this wealth I have made thee warden." (D. G. Rossetti, Eden Bower, Poems xxi). Sense 3, guardian of the person and lands of an orphan heir (obsolete, c1290-1700): 1385 "Thus here wardeynys wolde they disceyue." (G. Chaucer, Legend of Good Women 753); 1579 "Wardeine most properly is he that hath the wardship or keeping of an heire" (Rastell, Exposition Termes of Lawes 97b). Sense 4.a, regent or viceroy (obsolete except historical, a1400-); 4.b, governor of a town, province or district, Warden of the Marches (1297-1917): 1470-85 "And sire Brastias was maade wardeyn to wayte vpon the northe fro Trent forwardes." (T. Malory, Morte d'Arthur i. viii. 44). Sense 5, a guild officer, 1389-: 1640 "Next year wee will haue him warden Of our societie." (P. Massinger, Parliament of Love iv. ii. 57). Sense 6.a, the person having the direction or oversight of some work or enterprise (obsolete, 1398-1601): 1601 "Pythagoras, a great maister and warden of these exercises." (P. Holland, trans. Pliny). Sense 2.d, a gatekeeper, porter, sentinel, now rare, a1250-: 1801 "Fit warden of the sorcery-gate" (R. Southey, Thalaba II. xii. 314); 1894 "Female wardens made a fit outpost for this palace of many women." (R. L. Stevenson, In the South Seas iv. iii. 319). Sense 8.a, custodian of a building, esp. a temple or church (obsolete, 1290-1642): 1642 "The good Herald..is a Warden of the temple of Honour." (T. Fuller, Holy State ii. xxii. 141). Sense 11, head of a college, school or hospital, 1575-: 1855 "..a fitting residence for a warden." (A. Trollope, The Warden i. 3). Sense 12, prison keeper, c1330-: 1330 "Wiþ wardeyns þat hem vndertoke." (R. Mannyng, Chronicle Wace 13112). Sense 7.c, an air-raid warden, 1936-: 1936 "An organization of 'air raid wardens' to give immediate information and to help in dealing with fires caused by incendiary bombs." (Times 11 July 16/4); latest noun quotation 1978 "A tin-hatted Air Raid Warden was hurrying along the street... The Warden hurried on." (E. Malpass, Wind brings up Rain xxvi. 232). VERB warden v., transitive, to watch over or guard as a warden, spec. to watch over or patrol (a nature reserve, etc.), also intransitive to act as a wildlife warden, 1910-: 1910 "To warden the waves was his further bent." (T. Hardy, The Dynasts ii. i. vi. 165); 1971 "Having wardened at the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds reserve at Loch Garten, may I enlarge upon the letter from M. S. M. Burns?" (Times 7 May 17/7); 1974 "It would be wardened and visited regularly to prevent vandalism and litter." (Oxford Times 4 January 7/6); 1982 "The eyres are well wardened against egg collectors." (Lakeland Echo 18 March 5). A borrowing from Old French wardein, north-eastern variant of guarden (OED etymology). The verb is formed within English by conversion from the noun. OED frequency: noun about 2 occurrences per million words; verb about 0.06. No Old English evidence for either. The OED also lists a separate warden n.2 (a baking pear), not used here.

definition: OED falter v.1, the senses in use. 1.a Of a person or his or her steps; also of a horse: to stumble, stagger; to walk with an unsteady gait. 2.a To stumble in one's speech; to speak hesitatingly or incoherently; to stammer. usage_notes: OED befit v. first published 1887, not fully revised; formed within English by derivation from be- prefix 2 + fit v.1; earliest recorded c1460 (Middle English). Manuscript: Chapter 1 'the exact splendours that befit high merrymaking' (finite transitive verb); elsewhere 'a befitting hunting perch', 'a befitting post from which to loose an arrow', and 'a befitting hunt to herald a prince’s coming of age' (participial form modifying a noun). All are applications of OED sense 1. The supplied OED verb quotations explicitly attest the participial form used adjectivally: 1598 'a certaine naturall instinct befitting this office' and 1843 'The various duties befitting his princely station'; these establish the historical grammar without requiring a separate adjective-entry search. The precise manuscript noun combinations have not been independently attested. OED source PDFs supplied by author: etymology, factsheet, meaning & use. Tier 3 assigned by author.
quote: He ought..to haue a certaine naturall instinct befitting this office.
source: Oxford English Dictionary, befit v., sense 1, Meaning & use
locator: 1598 quotation, R. Barret, Theorike & Practike of Moderne Warres

job: stirring; in motion, active, or excited (adverb)
definition: OED astir adv., under 'Stirring': sense a, out of bed, up and moving about (from 1823); sense b, generally in motion (from 1856); sense c, figuratively in excitement (from 1837).
usage_notes: OED astir adv., first published 1885, not fully revised; formed within English by compounding a prep.1 + stir n.1; OED etymology suggests possible anglicization from Scots asteer. Earliest OED attestation 1823. Four manuscript uses: Chapter 1 'the readying was full astir' (bustling preparation; compare sense c); later 'the wood was astir with the noise of its bestial throng' (place active/in motion, compare sense b); 'the Darógan is astir' (awake or active, sense a or b, context dependent); 'He found the wildwood quick astir' (movement/activity, sense b). OED 1870 quotation 'The village is astir with sea-faring men' supports a place + be astir with + noun construction; it does not attest the full collocation astir with the noise. The modifiers full astir and quick astir have not been independently attested by the supplied OED examples; the 1833 example 'The whole village was early astir' shows a modifier but not these two. OED classifies astir as adverb even in these predicative constructions. Tier 3 assigned by author; evidence from user-supplied OED factsheet, etymology and Meaning & use pages.
quote: The village is astir with sea-faring men.
source: Oxford English Dictionary, astir adv., Meaning & use, sense c
locator: 1870, F. R. Wilson, Architectural Survey of Churches, Lindisfarne 34

job: to rejoice, delight in, or take pleasure in something (verb)
definition: OED joy v., sense 2.b: intransitive, to rejoice or delight in doing something or in something, with in (also of, at, with), from 1303. Sense 2.a: intransitive, to feel or manifest joy, be glad, rejoice or exult, from c1325. Sense 4.a (from c1330) concerns deriving enjoyment from or enjoying something, especially transitive, and is supplementary rather than the primary match.
usage_notes: OED joy v., first published 1901, not fully revised; borrowed from Old French joir, earliest use c1260 (Middle English). Six manuscript occurrences of the verb, three joyed and three joy: Chapter 1 'the valefolk joyed in every bit'; Chapter 1 'the valefolk joyed most in the Youngling Glade'; Chapter 2 'she joyed in the thought of it'; Chapter 5 'fain was he to joy in their bond and banter yet again'; Chapter 11 'if to joy in the sport and brotherhood'; later 'I joy not in the tidings I must now lay bare'. All use joy in + noun phrase, positive or negated, matching OED sense 2.b. The supplied OED sense heading explicitly lists 'in' among its prepositions; the selected 1885 quotation documents the historical inflected form joyed with a different preposition and belongs to sense 2.a, so it is not direct evidence for the complete joy in construction. Noun joy is a separate OED research target. Tier 3 assigned by author; evidence based on supplied OED etymology, factsheet, and Meaning & use PDF.
quote: She had..sympathised and sorrowed and joyed with them.
source: Oxford English Dictionary, joy v., Meaning & use, sense 2.a (supporting inflected form); sense 2.b (construction with in)

job: full of frolic; gay, merry, or mirthful (adjective)
definition: OED frolicsome adj., single recorded sense: full of frolic; gay, merry, mirthful. Historical examples apply the adjective to delight (1699), manner (1791), malice (1807), and people (1863).
usage_notes: OED frolicsome adj., first published 1898, not fully revised; formed within English by derivation from frolic v. or frolic n. + -some suffix. Earliest recorded use 1699 (Early Modern English). The manuscript has one use in Chapter 1: 'In every corner, the readying was full astir, and the valefolk joyed in every bit—from the tumblers’ tricks in the boughs to the jester-troupes and their frolicsome buffoonery.' Frolicsome is an attributive adjective modifying buffoonery, meaning merry, playful, lively behavior. The OED's 1791 'playful and frolicksome manner' and 1807 'frolicksome malice' corroborate use for qualities or forms of conduct, but do not attest the exact manuscript phrase frolicsome buffoonery. User-supplied OED factsheet, etymology, and Meaning & use PDFs. Tier 3 assigned by author.
quote: in the most playful and frolicksome manner.
source: Oxford English Dictionary, frolicsome adj., Meaning & use
locator: 1791, J. Boswell, Life of Johnson, vol. I, Dedication

job: comic or farcical conduct characteristic of a buffoon; ridiculous but amusing behavior (noun)
definition: OED buffoonery n., sole sense: behaviour typical or characteristic of a buffoon; silliness, farce, now especially ridiculous but amusing behaviour; also an instance of this.
usage_notes: OED buffoonery n., revised 2025; formed within English by derivation from buffoon n. + -ery suffix, compared to French bouffonnerie and Italian buffoneria. Earliest OED use 1589. The manuscript has one occurrence in Chapter 1: 'In every corner, the readying was full astir, and the valefolk joyed in every bit—from the tumblers’ tricks in the boughs to the jester-troupes and their frolicsome buffoonery.' Here buffoonery is a mass noun referring to the troupe's playful comic performances, not necessarily derogatory. The 1589 quotation links buffoonery to amusing an audience, offering a historical comparison; the exact collocation frolicsome buffoonery is not established by the OED. Frolicsome was separately researched in evidence #86, register #86. Source: author-supplied OED factsheet, etymology, and Meaning & use PDFs. Tier 3 assigned by author.
quote: There was another kind of poeme, inuented onely to make sport, & to refresh the company with a maner of Buffonry or counterfaiting of merry speaches.
source: Oxford English Dictionary, buffoonery n., Meaning & use, sole sense

job: glad, well-pleased, willing, eager or desirous (adjective); gladly or willingly, especially with would (adverb)
definition: OED fain adj. & adv., adjective A.1.a: glad, rejoiced, well-pleased (Old English onward); A.2.a: glad or content with an infinitive, especially under circumstances (from c1330); A.2.b: necessitated, obliged (later development, not the usual manuscript sense); A.3.a: disposed, inclined or willing, eager, with to, for, or infinitive (archaic or dialectal); adverb B: gladly, willingly, with pleasure, often in would (had) fain, otherwise obsolete or archaic.
usage_notes: OED fain adj. & adv., first published 1894, not fully revised; inherited from Germanic, cognate with Old English fægen/fagen, Old Saxon fagan and Old Norse feginn; attested from Old English before 1150. Manuscript study counted 23 standalone occurrences of fain: adjectival 'anyone fain to amble', 'she was fain to see', 'fain she was to sing it', 'fain was he to joy', 'fain for a bit of sport', 'his heart full fain for adventure', and 'For longer than he was fain' (A.2.a or A.3.a as contextualized); adverbial 'would fain thank you', 'I would fain know' (B). 'the wōdlund beasts fed full and fain' has a plausible sense of gladness or pleasure but its exact construction and part-of-speech assignment remain unverified, not a demonstrated OED idiom. OED documents full fain and glad and fain but not necessarily the exact phrase fed full and fain. Manuscript compound flesh-fain is a separate potentially coined formation, not counted in the 23 standalone uses and not independently attested by the supplied OED materials. Selected 1874 historical quotation demonstrates would fain + bare infinitive; precise manuscript constructions are not all separately historically attested. Tier 4 assigned by author. User supplied OED factsheet, etymology and three-page Meaning & use PDF.
quote: Those who would fain divide the community into two great castes.

job: to walk or move at a relaxed, leisurely pace; to traverse a route by ambling (verb)
definition: OED amble v. sense 2.a: intransitive, of a person, to walk with a relaxed or leisurely pace, originally with a motion reminiscent of a horse's amble (from c1576). Sense 3: transitive, to pursue or follow a way or course by ambling, including a named route or place (from 1607). Sense 1.a concerns gait of a horse, and 1.b riding a horse, neither required for the three manuscript verb uses.
usage_notes: OED amble v., revised 2020, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Old French ambler, ultimately from Latin ambulare. Earliest evidence 1310, Middle English, for a horse's ambling gait. Three manuscript uses: 'anyone fain to amble the southern rim' (transitive with route as direct object, sense 3), 'Ambling forth, she lifted a verse' (present participle, intransitive sense 2.a), and 'as they ambled forth' (past tense, sense 2.a). The OED's transitive sense 3 includes examples of ambling a road, streets, and fields; the exact southern rim phrase and amble forth combinations are not independently attested by supplied quotations. Both noun and verb forms of amble were researched separately at Tier 3 and have separate OED entries. OED PDFs supplied by author: etymology, factsheet and two-page meaning & use.
quote: She was a common enough sight around the town, ambling the fields with her metal detector.
source: Oxford English Dictionary, amble v., Meaning & use, sense 3
locator: 2005 quotation, J. Kelly, Moon Tunnel, p. 23

job: a smooth, easy gait of a horse; a slow or leisurely walk or stroll (noun)
definition: OED amble n., sense 1: smooth or easy gait of a horse or other quadruped (attested c1405 onward). Sense 2: a slow, relaxed or leisurely gait or pace of a person (from 1607). Sense 3: an instance of a leisurely walk or stroll, originally also a ride at a smooth or easy gait (from 1825).
usage_notes: OED amble n., revised 2020; of multiple origins, partly borrowed from Middle French amble (horse's gait) and partly formed within English by conversion from amble v. Earliest OED noun attestation c1405, Middle English. Two manuscript noun uses: 'The grass waved vivid and bid them take a barefoot amble' (countable noun, a leisurely walk, sense 3); 'He kept his steed at an even amble' (the horse's gait, sense 1). The OED documents both meanings, but does not independently attest the precise manuscript collocations barefoot amble or even amble. Separate OED noun entry and evidence from amble v. (Evidence #89); Tier 3 assigned by author. User-supplied OED etymology, factsheet and two-page meaning & use PDF.

job: a traveller by road, especially one who goes on foot (noun)
definition: OED wayfarer n.: a traveller by road, especially one who goes on foot; sole recorded sense, attested from c1430 to modern use. OED records both singular and plural forms.
usage_notes: OED wayfarer n. revised 2015; formed within English by compounding way n.1 + farer n.; compare Old English wegfarend, of the same general meaning. Earliest OED evidence c1430 (Middle English). Four manuscript uses: Chapter 1 'great kings and wayfarers of the wider world'; Chapter 7 'long forsaken and eschewed of wayfarers'; Chapter 9 'Many a footsore wayfarer stopped to take their rest at the edge of the wold'; Chapter 9 'two wayfarers came in'. All refer to people on journeys, the footsore example particularly implying travel on foot. Historical OED examples include hungry wayfarer (1836), wayfarers (1896), and single wayfarer (2001). The OED does not independently attest the full manuscript combination many a footsore wayfarer. Tier 4 assigned by author; supplied OED factsheet, etymology and Meaning & use PDFs.

job: limited, scant, rare or insufficient (adjective); hardly, barely, or sparingly (adverb)
definition: OED scarce adj. & adv., adjective A.1.a: scanty or restricted in amount (1297–1596, obsolete); A.3: existing or accessible in deficient quantity (from c1374); A.4.a: existing in limited numbers, seldom seen (from 1398). Adverb B.1: scantily or sparingly (c1300–1450, obsolete, rare); B.2.a: barely, hardly, only just, not quite (from 1413, now archaic or literary); B.2.c: with reference to time, barely or only just (from 1513, now archaic or literary); B.3: seldom or rarely (1596–1663, obsolete).
usage_notes: OED scarce adj. & adv., first published 1910 and not fully revised; borrowed from Old Northern French scars/escars. First recorded c1290 (Middle English). Manuscript study found 24 occurrences, all written scarce, with various grammatical functions. Common adverbial B.2.a usages include 'scarce any beyond the Vale', 'scarce a Feifýren remains', 'scarce one in seven generations', 'could scarce contain', 'could scarce understand', 'I scarce remember', 'I can scarce fathom it', and 'they would but scarce miss each other'. Time reference 'scarce a fortnight ago' compares with B.2.c. 'trees scattered scarce across the way' may reflect historical adverb B.1, meaning sparingly, rather than the modern hardly sense, but is only a tentative match. Quantity/extent expressions include 'a scarce few days' and 'scarce many winters', whose exact historical constructions are not independently attested by supplied OED quotations; attribution to adjective or adverb varies with syntax. 'scarce their hearts could contain' also has unusual adverb placement and is documented as manuscript usage, not independent historical formula. The OED groups adjective and adverb under the same entry; no separate adverb search is required. Tier 1 assigned by author; source supplied as OED etymology, factsheet, and six-page Meaning & use PDF.
quote: I ran as I never ran before, scarce missing the direction of my flight.

job: a clump of bushes, brushwood, or briers; a thicket (noun)
definition: OED brake n.2, sole meaning: a clump of bushes, brushwood, or briers; a thicket. Also used attributively (as brake-axe). Recorded from c1440, Middle English, through later literary and landscape descriptions.
usage_notes: OED brake n.2, first published 1888, not fully revised. Etymology uncertain: compare Middle Low German brake, but OED says the historical relationship is unknown. Manuscript has six singular noun uses for thickets or tangled undergrowth: Chapter 1 'entangled with brake and briar, nettle and bramble'; elsewhere 'Through brake and underwood she led forth their unlikely company'; 'Athwart the brake and briar, Prince Caelurún fared forth'; 'At the edge of the weald along the brake and greenwood'; Chapter 7 'entangled thick with brake and thistle'; Chapter 8 'through the wildwood brake and bramble'. These uses match the OED noun's thicket/brushwood sense. OED examples show brakes alongside thickets (1625), undergrowth of shrubs (1667), and brakes of fern and fallen trees (1777), supporting the vegetation context but not independently establishing each exact manuscript pairing. OED brake n.2 is distinct from other brake noun entries. Tier 4 assigned by author. Evidence supplied as OED etymology, factsheet and Meaning & use PDFs.

job: several, various, or of differing kinds; predicatively, numerous or diverse (adjective)
definition: OED sundry adj. & pron., adjective II.5.a 'a number of, several' (from c1275) and II.6.a.i 'of various kinds; varied, diverse, manifold' when modifying a plural noun (from a1325). I.4, distinct or separate, attested from a1393 and now rare, is related but not primary here. OED II.5.b obsolete partitive use, equivalent to 'sundry of', provides a comparison for 'sundry the' (a1325–1780). The OED attests predicative inverted 'how ... sondry are' (1586) and predicative 'are sundry' (1668).
usage_notes: Inherited from Germanic, recorded in Old English; cognate with/formationally related to Middle Low German sünderich/sünderch and Old High German suntarīg, from bases of sunder and -y. The user's full-manuscript scan found five appearances, all adjective: Chapter 1 'Sundry are the beasts of Forrumir Vale, and wondrous'; Chapter 8 'he withstood sundry perils and snares'; Chapter 11 'a long marble passage with sundry other doors'; Chapter 11 the Seer's 'Sundry the titles I bore in the course of ages'; Chapter 11 'Sundry are the whimsies and ferlies of the mighty Darógan'. The ordinary plural-noun modifiers match OED II.5.a / II.6.a.i. The inverted 'Sundry are...' has a close 1586 quotation under II.6.a.i. For the Seer's 'Sundry the titles I bore', the author accepts either 'Many were the titles I bore' (elliptical predicative inversion with unspoken 'were', ellipsis itself not independently verified) or 'Several of the titles I bore' (compare obsolete partitive II.5.b); retain both readings without declaring one settled. OED's 1588 'sundrie the coste townes' illustrates historical partitive form but does not establish the elliptical inverted form. No grammar.csv addition authorised. Tier 4 assigned by author. OED meaning and etymology data supplied by author as text.

job: to wait; linger; delay or put off an action; remain temporarily in a place; continue in a state (verb)
definition: OED tarry v.: 1 transitive, to delay, defer, put off or prolong something (c1320–1583, obsolete); 2 transitive, to detain or keep someone waiting (1340–1609, obsolete); 3.a intransitive, to delay, linger, loiter or wait before doing something (a1375–); 3.b intransitive, to wait in expectation, often with till or for (1390–); 4.a intransitive, to remain or continue in a state (a1450–1814, obsolete); 4.b intransitive, to stay or sojourn temporarily in a place (c1400–1877, archaic except U.S.); 5.a transitive, to wait for or await (a1475–, archaic); 5.b transitive, to outstay a given time (?a1500, obsolete).
usage_notes: OED tarry v. supplied by User: earliest overall evidence c1320 in a translation of Bonaventura's Meditations; first intransitive quotation a1375 (c1350) in William of Palerne. Other OED quotations include ME 1390 'Hath taried til thei were aslepe' (Gower, Confessio Amantis); EMdE 1611 'Why tarie the wheeles of his charets?' (King James Bible, Judges v.28); EMdE 1611 'She that taried at home, diuided the spoile' (King James Bible, Psalms lxviii.12); LMdE 1849 'He saw that if he tarried the royal cavalry would soon be in his rear' (Macaulay, History of England); LMdE 1892 'we had no time to tarry' (Nation, New York, 27 October). OED says now chiefly literary in Great Britain, still colloquial in U.S.; 0.7 occurrences per million words in modern written English. Entry not fully revised. Eleven appearances in Wōdlund Manuscript, Chapters 1, 2, 10, 11, 12: 'The days of the feria tarried beyond measure'; 'She tarried'; 'tarrying a spell'; 'They tarried in front of the door'; 'Tarry not in the garden'; Chapter 11 'We shall tarry but a while longer'; 'I must tarry before I take my leave'; 'tarried before the crystal thrones'; 'Tarried you all this long-while in Míræv-elû?'; 'the Andiān tarried'; 'we have tarried over long'. Some exact manuscript sentence patterns are not independently attested by the OED quotations supplied. Tier 4 assigned by User. job: an initial effort in learning or practicing an art (noun); more broadly a trial, attempt, or test
definition: OED assay n., III.16: 'A first tentative effort, in learning or practice' (?1570–1677, obsolete); III.13: 'An attempt, an endeavour' (c1386 onward, archaic). The manuscript instance most closely reflects III.16, with III.13 also relevant.
usage_notes: OED assay n. (not fully revised): 23 senses, 16 labelled obsolete; first evidence 1330 (Robert Mannyng, ME). Borrowed from Old French assai/assay, variant of essai/essay, ultimately Latin exagium 'weighing', extended to examination and trial. General assay largely displaced by essay from late 16th century, while metal-testing and related scientific senses persist. OED group I: trying or trial (I.1), tribulation (I.2), experiment (I.3), experience (I.4), faculty of judging (I.5). II: metal test (II.6.a); biological test (II.6.b, from 1922); matter to be assayed (II.7); official inspection (II.8); hunting inspection of deer fat (II.9); tasting (II.10); figurative foretaste (II.11); tasting food before a ruler (II.12.a) and 'cup of assay' (II.12.b). III: attempt (III.13), fullest effort (III.14), assault (III.15), first learning/practice effort (III.16), sample (III.17). IV: approved quality (IV.18.a), metallic fineness (IV.18.b), character (IV.19), measured depth (IV.20). OED Phrases includes obsolete 'at all assays' (at every crisis or on all occasions; alternatively armed and ready), not present in manuscript and not registered separately. Manuscript: one noun occurrence in Chapter 1, 'the elders waited in earnest, holding dear their youthful assay of the ancient arts', referring to young feylings showing newly learned powers; contextual sense III.16 most precise, III.13 also possible. The precise phrase 'youthful assay' is not attested in supplied OED quotations. The noun has supplied OED quotations through PDE (biological assay in 1961), although III.16 itself ends in 1677; hence noun entry era_range ME to PDE. Tier 4 explicitly assigned by User. OED Meaning & use, Factsheet, and Etymology supplied by User as text.

historical_spelling: wende; wenden; wendest; wente; went; wended
job: to turn or change direction (original sense); to go, travel, proceed, follow a course, or make one's way, sometimes unhurriedly or circuitously (verb)
definition: OED wend v.1: branch I 'to turn, change', with I.1.a–d (turn objects, oneself, or thoughts), I.2.a–d (alter or direct mind/will), I.3.a–c (alter, translate, pass into a state), I.4.a–b (transform), I.5 (events taking a course), I.6.a–b (return; wind changes direction), I.7.a–b (nautical tacking). Branch II 'to go, proceed', especially II.8.b (persons or groups journey or travel, OE–), II.8.c (material or immaterial things proceed in a direction, OE–), II.8.d (transitively follow a way/course, esp. 'wend one's way', c1225–). Also II.8.a reflexive betake oneself (OE–); II.8.e go to a place for a purpose; II.8.f go on errand/voyage (obsolete); II.8.g cause to move or direct; II.9.a–c depart, die, or cease to be present (obsolete); II.10 descend or fall (obsolete); II.11.a–b carry on affairs or live in a state (obsolete).
usage_notes: OED wend v.1 Factsheet and Etymology supplied by User; 31 meanings, 23 labelled obsolete; earliest evidence Old English, modern frequency c. 0.4 per million written words, now somewhat literary. Germanic inheritance; cognate with Frisian, Dutch, German and Scandinavian turning verbs, formed causatively from an ablaut grade of the base of wind v.1. Sense development 'turn' -> 'turn in a direction in order to go' -> 'go'; in later standard use 'wend'/'wended' may imply an indirect or meandering or unhurried route, a nuance not necessarily in early use. Middle English went from wend became the suppletive past tense of go; the re-formed past wended developed by the end of the 16th century. Distinctions between go and wend, and between turning and going, can be ambiguous in early evidence. The manuscript contains 20 word-family occurrences: 19 verbal wend/wended in Chapters 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 11, and 1 nominalized 'wending' in Chapter 13. Seven wend, twelve wended, one wending. Movement II.8.b: 'wended home', 'wended valeward again', 'wend apace', 'wend right', 'wended on deeper yet', 'the way that I wend'. Direct-object path/way II.8.d: 'wended her way', 'wended their path', 'wend his way beyond', 'wended the knotted wild', 'wended their way east', 'wended his way west'; 'wended the knotted wild' (wilderness as direct object) is not independently exemplified by the OED quotations supplied. Immateral or route subject II.8.c: 'let her musings wend', 'his path would wend', 'the fleetest course wended', 'let his thoughts wend'; OED II.8.c has 1593 'My thoughts ... wend all awrie' and 1995 'where her younger daughter’s thoughts wended'. Figurative return: 'wended back into the lore that made her' (compare II.8.b with back, and obsolete I.6.a figurative returning); physical return 'wended back to where he began'. Chapter 1 'Wended on her way, has she?' is past-tense motion with 'on her way'. OED II.8.d has 2011 'We wended our way through picnicking Parisians' as a late quotation. The Chapter 13 'beyond the usual wending' is nominal, and its possible separate noun entry was not supplied; do not merge it silently into the verb entry as an independently attested noun or assign a separate tier. 'Wend one's way' is a transparent construction, not a separate idiom record. Author assigns Tier 4 to the submitted verb.
quote: Þa ðær wendon forð wlance þegenas, unearge men efston georne.
source: Oxford English Dictionary, wend v.1, Meaning & use, II.8.b
locator: Old English, Battle of Maldon (1942), line 205

historical_spelling: wendinge; wendynge; wendyng; wendynges; weendyng; wendingges; wendings
job: the action of going or journeying; a journey; also historically a turn or change, nautical tacking, or the meandering course of a road or river (noun)
definition: OED wending n., sense 3 'A journey' (1340–1500, obsolete), the strongest match for the manuscript's 'the usual wending'. Also sense 2.a (c1330–), the act of going, proceeding or wandering, now somewhat literary. Other senses in this OED noun entry: 1.a (Old English–1851, obsolete) turning, a twist, a bend or a change; 1.b (?c1588–, nautical, now rare) turning a vessel, especially tacking; 2.b (1826–) the meandering progress of a river or road.
usage_notes: User-supplied OED wending n. Meaning & use spans OE to PDE: earliest quotation eOE in King Ælfred's translation of Gregory, Pastoral Care, referring to turning; 2.a examples include c1330 Guy of Warwick and 2001 S. Heaney, Electric Light; 2.b from 1826 to 2011; sense 3 only 1340–1500. OED Factsheet and Etymology for this separate noun were not supplied; no etymology is independently asserted. One manuscript noun occurrence in Chapter 13: 'The last snow of spring was yet melting, and, for the mud and ice, the wayfare proved slow. They were some few days beyond the usual wending.' Context indicates they are some days beyond the duration expected for the customary journey; exact 'usual wending' combination is not independently attested by supplied OED quotations. historical_spelling: lār; lare; laar; lair; lear; loore
job: teaching, learning or accumulated knowledge; in later use, a body of traditional facts, narratives, anecdotes, or beliefs (noun)
definition: OED lore n.1: sense 1 instruction, teaching or a lesson (OE–, now archaic/dialect); sense 2.a doctrine or teaching, chiefly religious or moral (OE–, now poetic/archaic); 2.b plural doctrines/precepts/ordinances (OE–1580, obsolete); 2.c creed or religion (a1225–1560, obsolete); 2.d rule of behaviour (c1400–85, obsolete); 3 advice, counsel, instruction or command (a1300–); 4 vague spoken information, story or language (a1375–1420, obsolete); 5.a learning, scholarship, erudition and, especially in later use, the body of traditional facts, anecdotes or beliefs relating to a subject (a1225–); 5.b a body of knowledge or a science (c1290–1551, obsolete). Manuscript's six uses chiefly match 5.a; 2.a is a plausible secondary doctrinal comparison for the Elder Fire.
usage_notes: OED lore n.1 Factsheet, Meaning & use and Etymology supplied by User. Earliest known use Old English; one Germanic inheritance, Old English lār (strong feminine), related to Old Saxon lêra and Old High German lêra, from Germanic *laizâ and ultimately root lais-; compare learn v. OED entry not fully revised; modern written-English frequency about 3 per million. Six noun occurrences in Wōdlund Manuscript, all singular/mass-noun: Chapter 1 'wended back into the lore that made her' (traditional accounts); Chapter 1 'the telling of the lore and laurelled deeds from days long past' (inherited stories); Chapter 2 'its wont of spellcraft and lore' (learned magical knowledge); Chapter 4 'borne of shadowy tongues and vanished lore' (lost tradition or remembered knowledge); Chapter 5 'the prophecies and deep lore of the Elder Fire' (specialized spiritual knowledge, potential 2.a doctrine as secondary reading); Chapter 5 'the eldest of Feifýren lore and legend' (traditional narrative). OED 5.a expressly documents the later traditional-belief use and gives 1766 'Skill'd in legendary lore' as illustration. No exact full manuscript phrase was independently attested as an idiom. Latest dated quotation supplied for this noun entry: 1901 (LMdE) under 5.a, though OED reports present-day use; per register's dated-evidence rule era_range is OE to LMdE, not an inference of PDE quotation from frequency data. Tier 4 assigned by author. No separate idiom or grammar pattern requested.
quote: Skill'd in legendary lore.
source: Oxford English Dictionary, lore n.1, Meaning & use, sense 5.a
locator: 1766, O. Goldsmith, A Ballad [The Hermit], in The Vicar of Wakefield: A Tale, vol. I, viii, 72

job: a dwelling or abode, a settlement such as a village or hamlet, and in specific regional senses a farm, dairy farm, or enclosed piece of land (noun)
definition: OED wick n.2 (headword 'wick', not lamp-wick), four senses: 1, an abode, dwelling or dwelling-place in general (OE–1300, obsolete); 2, a town, village or hamlet (OE onward, obsolete or dialect, surviving in -wich and -wick placenames); 3, a farm, especially a dairy farm (OE onward, now local); 4, an enclosed piece of land or close (1301–1811, local and obsolete). Manuscript 'woad wykes' most plausibly refers to dwellings (sense 1) or small settlements (sense 2); no clear evidence it denotes specifically dairy farms (3) or enclosed fields (4).
usage_notes: OED wick n.2 Meaning & use, Factsheet and Etymology supplied by User; first known use OE; entry not yet fully revised, modern-written frequency about 0.2 per million. Old English wíc (masculine or feminine) has Frisian, Saxon, Dutch and High German cognates. OED considers the underlying Germanic family apparently from Latin vīcus ('row of houses, quarter of a city, street, village'); inherited into English from Germanic, ultimately related to Greek οἶκος. Manuscript plural spelling 'wykes' occurs twice, with no singular 'wyke' occurrence: Chapter 1 'They bided amidst the heather and bilberry out on Seer’s Moor, in their woad wykes'; Chapter 3 'Fast-bound and burdened, he rode through mist and woad wykes'. Context describes places inhabited by the woadfolk and later passed through on the moor. Cannot determine from manuscript alone whether individual dwellings or entire hamlets; both OED senses 1 and 2 recorded as possibilities. OED has 'Wyke' in ?a1461 'Bondmannys Wyke' under enclosure sense 4; spellings 'wickes' in 1600 under village sense 2 and 1594 under dairy sense 3. Historical spelling 'wyke' is documented, but exact plural 'wykes' is not verified by the OED quotations supplied. 'Woad wykes' is a transparent modifier plus noun, not a pre-PDE non-compositional idiom. OED sense 3 includes a late 1879 quotation and sense 2 contains an 1885 note, so latest provided historical evidence is LMdE; OED describes some senses as still local/dialect but no PDE-dated quotation was provided. Tier 4 assigned by User.

job: to mark a deed, person, virtue, or achievement as honoured, distinguished, illustrious, or crowned with laurels
definition: OED laurelled adj., sense a (1683–): literally adorned, crowned, or wreathed with laurel, hence figuratively honoured or illustrious. Manuscript 'laurelled deeds' means heroic or illustrious deeds celebrated or remembered from the past, figurative sense a; sense b does not fit.

quote: The Trophies of my Lawrell'd Honesty Shou'd bar me from forsaking this bad World.

definition: Emma Lazarus, 'Success': 'Palm-bearing, laureled deeds that live forever,' refers to glorious accomplishments preserved in remembrance. job: to link a later action to a prior event or circumstance: on that ground, consequently, or following what happened (adverb)
definition: OED thereupon adv. 2.a: upon that in time or order, on that being done or said, directly after that (a1400–); 2.b: on that ground, as a consequence (1534–, archaic). MED thē̆r-upon adv. 2(a): subsequently, then; 2(b): in response to that; 2(c): as a result, consequently or on that basis; 2(d): moreover or in addition. MED 2(b) covers responding to a circumstance and MED 2(d) additive sense, earliest provided citation a1225 (c1200) Vices & Virtues, which is not the causal meaning. Its form analysis says the β forms show reduction of the first element, the γ forms are aphetic (loss of the initial vowel, probably from metanalysis), and enon apparently shows further reduction of the initial vowel. Its account of semantic development says that beside use of position, state or direction (senses 1 and 2) the adverb developed the temporal sense at once, immediately already in Old English (sense 3); that in Middle English this sense came to function as a pragmatic marker, foregrounding important events in the narrative and moving it forward; that, in an independent development, the temporal sense was weakened in the late Middle English period from immediately to shortly, in a little while (sense 4), compare presently adv. and soon adv.; that this weakened sense became the more common use in early modern English; and that interpersonal use as a marker of attentiveness developed out of the temporal use in this period (see anan int.). Chapter 5 (1): As the dance-troupe took its place on the stage, officers of the hall began to make ready the lower feast tables and the high board of the King. There with him sat his counsellors and honourable guests—the great lords of Gadólrun and Bendithel. The match to a sense is an inference. High board of the King is a noun phrase naming the table at which the King sits at the feast, set beside the lower feast tables; it is matched to sense II.8.a, a table used for meals or spread for a meal, which the OED marks chiefly poetic. The OED quotation Afor mete, whenne the bordes er sette and made redye (c1440) has the bordes made ready before the meal, as the officers make ready the tables in the manuscript. Not matched: II.10.a (a table at which a council is held), whose first quotation has the phrase highe boorde of thee counsell (1576), because the manuscript scene is a feast and the counsellors are guests seated with the King, though a council sense cannot be ruled out from the OED pages alone. History (OED Etymology): a word inherited from Germanic. The OED says the relationship between the two is uncertain and the sense table is doubtful; it adds that Old English had a doubtful sense table and that the sense is common already in the 12th century. Early Middle English tenden corresponded to an Old English *tęndan (in compounds ontęndan, atęndan, fortęndan, to set fire to, kindle, and in verbal noun tęnding, Napier Contrib. to OE. Lexic.), corresponding to Gothic tandjan, Danish tænde, Swedish tända; causative of *tindan strong verb (ablaut series tind-, tand-, tund-), to be on fire, burn, glow, represented by Middle High German zinden strong verb, in same sense. In that case, tend (teend, teen, teyne) and tind (tynd, tīnd, tin, tīne, tyne) are two distinct but parallel and synonymous formations from the same root verb.
